questions.q: In the rule-of-thumb formula C ≈ 6ND, what do N and D represent?
options: N is GPU count, D is dataset size in gigabytes
N is the number of model parameters, D is the number of training tokens
N is the number of layers, D is the learning rate decay factor
N is the number of epochs, D is the batch size
questions.explain: C ≈ 6ND estimates total training FLOPs as roughly 6 times the parameter count (N) times the number of training tokens (D).

questions.q: What was the key finding of the Chinchilla scaling-law work?
options: Model architecture matters more than parameter count or data size
Many earlier large models were over-parameterized relative to their training data; compute-optimal training scales parameters and tokens together
Vocabulary size has no effect on training compute
Larger batch sizes always reduce total compute cost
questions.explain: Hoffmann et al. found that for a fixed compute budget, many large models would have performed better as smaller models trained on proportionally more tokens -- motivating balanced scaling of parameters and data.

questions.q: What does Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) measure?
options: The percentage of a model's parameters that are actively used at inference time
The fraction of a GPU's theoretical peak FLOPs actually achieved during real training
The ratio of training tokens to validation tokens
The number of GPUs used in a distributed training job
questions.explain: MFU is the fraction of a GPU's peak theoretical throughput you actually realize once communication, memory bandwidth, and pipeline stalls are accounted for.

questions.q: Why might a lab deliberately train a model past the 'compute-optimal' Chinchilla ratio, using more tokens per parameter than strictly optimal for training compute alone?
options: It is impossible to train at the compute-optimal ratio in practice
Doing so reduces the vocabulary size automatically
Smaller, more-trained models are cheaper to run at inference time once the model is deployed at scale
It eliminates the need for a data pipeline entirely
questions.explain: A smaller model trained on more tokens can match or exceed the quality of a larger, less-trained model while being cheaper to run at inference -- which matters once the model serves real traffic, not just during training.

questions.q: Two teams run the exact same FLOPs budget on the same GPU hardware, but Team A achieves 45% MFU and Team B achieves 20% MFU. What is the practical consequence for Team B?
options: Team B's model will have a larger vocabulary
Team B's run will take roughly twice as long in wall-clock GPU-hours to consume the same FLOPs budget
Team B's model will automatically use the Chinchilla-optimal ratio
There is no practical difference since the FLOPs budget is identical
questions.explain: Lower MFU means less of the GPU's peak throughput is actually realized, so consuming the same total FLOPs takes proportionally longer wall-clock time -- roughly doubling real-world cost at half the utilization.
